body:
Batteries age with every charge cycle, and that cannot be avoided, but you can slow it down considerably. A battery that is looked after can serve for many months, while one that is neglected may fade within weeks. The habits that matter are mostly simple: avoid extremes of temperature, charge sensibly, use quality chargers, lower the power, take shorter puffs, keep contacts clean, store devices properly and know when to replace a battery. This guide explains each habit, why it works, how much difference it makes, how the principles apply to different types of device and when it is time to retire a battery. It is written for adults aged 21 and over. Nicotine is addictive.

## How lithium-ion batteries age
Every time you charge and discharge a lithium-ion battery, tiny chemical changes reduce how much charge it can hold. Heat speeds these changes up, as does holding the battery at a full charge or letting it run completely flat. After a few hundred cycles, a battery may hold 80 percent or less of its original capacity. You cannot stop this, but you can slow it. The habits below reduce wear and keep the battery working longer.

## Avoid extremes of temperature
Leaving a device in a hot car or freezing outdoors reduces capacity. Heat is the biggest enemy of batteries, because it speeds up unwanted reactions inside the cell. Cold reduces the battery's performance temporarily, and charging a very cold battery can harm it. Keep the device in a pocket at body temperature, and let it reach room temperature before charging. Do not leave it on a windowsill or in direct sun.

## Charge sensibly
Charge when it is low, rather than letting it run completely flat, and unplug when full. Lithium-ion batteries prefer partial charges to deep ones, and they dislike sitting at 100 percent for long periods. A top-up whenever it is convenient is fine. You do not have to drain the battery first. If you do not need a full charge, a partial one is gentler on the cell.

## Use quality chargers
A decent cable and 5V adapter provide stable power. Cheap, unbranded chargers can deliver uneven power, and poor cables can overheat or limit current. Replace damaged cables. Use the charger recommended by the maker, or a reputable standard one. See [how to charge a disposable](/blog/how-to-charge-a-disposable/).

## Lower the power
Higher wattage and boost modes drain batteries faster. Use the lowest setting that gives a satisfying draw. Lower power means less current, less heat and slower wear. If your device has power modes, try a lower one for everyday use, and save the higher one for when you want it. See [ohms, watts and volts](/blog/what-are-ohms-watts-and-volts-in-vaping/).

## Take shorter puffs
Long, repeated puffs draw heavily on the battery and heat the coil. A short, gentle puff uses less energy, and it gives the coil time to re-saturate. Chain vaping is the hardest on both battery and coil. Spacing your puffs makes the battery last longer between charges and keeps flavor better.

## Keep it clean
Dirty contacts increase resistance and waste energy. Wipe the contacts between the battery and the pod or tank with a dry cotton bud. Keep the charging port free of lint. Liquid that leaks onto contacts can corrode them over time. A clean device works more efficiently.

## Store properly
If you will not use a device for weeks, store it at around half charge in a cool place. A fully charged battery stored for a long time loses capacity faster, and a fully discharged one can fall into a state where it will not charge. Keep it away from heat and moisture, and out of reach of children and pets.

## Replace worn batteries
Built-in batteries cannot be replaced, so when they fade, the device has reached end of life. Removable cells can be replaced with correctly rated ones, from a reputable source. See [battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/). Never mix old and new cells, or different brands, in the same device. Dispose of old batteries responsibly; see [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/).

## How batteries relate to puffs
See [mAh, puffs and battery life](/blog/mah-puffs-and-battery-life-how-they-relate/) for how capacity, power and puff counts fit together.

## A worked example
Two people buy the same rechargeable disposable. Person A leaves it in the car in summer, lets it run to zero every time and charges it overnight. Person B keeps it in a pocket, charges it when it is low and unplugs it when full. After three months, Person A's device holds noticeably less charge and sometimes fails to turn on. Person B's still lasts most of the day. The difference is not luck, it is habit.

## Signs your battery is wearing out
- It drains much faster than it used to.
- It takes longer to charge or never reaches full.
- It feels warm when idle.
- The device shuts off unexpectedly.
- There is any swelling, odor or leaking.

If you see any of the last three, stop using the device, and see [lithium battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/).

## Habits by device type
### Disposables
Charge before empty, avoid heat, and use gentle puffs. You cannot replace the battery, so the goal is to reach the end of the liquid before the battery fades.

### Pod systems
Charge when low, keep the pod seated properly and avoid leaving the device in a hot place. The battery usually outlasts several pods, but wears over time.

### Tank and mod systems
Use batteries with adequate ratings, keep them paired and rotated, and avoid running at the limit of the power. Check the wraps regularly.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Should I let the battery run flat before charging?
No. Modern batteries do not need it, and deep discharges can shorten life.

### Is overnight charging bad?
It is not recommended. It keeps the battery at full charge for hours and leaves it unattended.

### Does a cold device last less?
Yes, temporarily. Warm it to room temperature and it recovers.

### Will a bigger battery last longer?
It holds more energy, but power use matters too. See the article on mAh and puffs.

### How long do batteries last?
It varies with use. With good habits, many last for months to years of regular use, but every battery eventually wears out.

## Case studies
### The commuter
A commuter kept a device in a coat pocket, charged it each evening to full and let it run low during the day. After a year, it still lasted a full day. Lesson: moderate habits add up.

### The car dweller
Another customer left a device in a car dashboard. After a summer, its capacity had fallen by half. Lesson: heat is the biggest enemy.

### The high-power fan
A customer ran a mod at its maximum setting. The battery lasted half a day, and wore faster. After lowering the power by a third, it lasted most of the day, and the flavor was just as good. Lesson: more power is not always better.

## A simple battery care calendar
Daily: keep the device in a pocket, charge when low. Weekly: wipe contacts and the charging port. Monthly: check for swelling, dents and loose parts. Every few months: consider whether the battery still lasts long enough for your needs. If not, plan a replacement and dispose of the old device properly.

## When a new device is the better choice
If your battery now lasts only a fraction of the time, and you are charging constantly, a new device may be better value than persisting. The cost of a replacement is small compared with the time and frustration of a failing battery. When you replace, look for a reputable maker, a standard charging port and a battery size that suits your use. See [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/).

## Frequently asked questions about batteries
### Do cheap chargers shorten battery life?
They can, because they may deliver uneven power. A reputable charger protects the battery.

### Is it bad to charge to 100 percent?
Occasionally it is fine. Sitting at 100 percent for days is not ideal. Unplug when full.

### Does vaping less often make the battery last longer?
It slows the number of charge cycles, but age also matters. A battery loses capacity with time even when idle.

### Can I revive an old battery?
Not reliably. If it is failing, replace the device or the cell, and dispose of the old one properly.

## Putting it into practice this week
Pick three habits to start with. First, stop leaving the device in the car. Second, charge it when it is low, during the day, and unplug it when it is full. Third, lower the power one step, or take shorter puffs. These three changes alone will make a noticeable difference within a few weeks. Add the others over time, and keep track of how long a charge lasts, so that you can see the effect of what you change.

## Choosing devices with battery life in mind
When you buy a new device, look at the battery size, the charging port and the maker's reputation. A device with a modest battery and efficient design can outlast a larger one that wastes power. Read reviews that mention real-world battery life. Our [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/) pages list battery capacity where the maker provides it.
